Why the borrow checker says no: a field guide to lifetimes

by Jane Example, 20 September 2026

The borrow checker is not a wall. It is a very patient reviewer who has read every line you wrote and would like a word about three of them. Once you can hear what it is actually saying, most of the arguments stop.

Three rules

  • Every value has exactly one owner.
  • You may borrow it, but not while it is being changed.
  • A borrow may not outlive the thing it borrows.

The third is the one that produces the error everybody remembers, and it is the one a diagram helps with least. What helps is naming the scopes out loud.

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() > b.len() { a } else { b }
}

Lifetimes are not about how long a value lives. They are about how long a reference is allowed to.

The Rustonomicon is the long version, and the earlier post on ownership is the short one. Between them there is very little left that a compiler error will surprise you with.

None of this makes the first month easier. It makes the second month possible, which is a different and better claim, and it is the one worth making to somebody who is still reaching for clone on every other line.
